notes.heading: Bond enthalpy and why it is average
points: Breaking bonds absorbs energy (endothermic, ΔH positive); forming bonds releases energy (exothermic, ΔH negative).
Bond enthalpy: energy to break one mole of a bond in gaseous molecules, standard conditions, giving radicals (homolytic fission). Example: H2(g) → 2H•(g), +436 kJ mol⁻¹.
Values are averages over many compounds, since the same bond sits in different chemical environments, e.g. successive C–H breaks in CH4 differ (439, 462, 424, 338).
Bond enthalpy values are in section 12 of the data booklet.
Calculated ΔH differs from experiment: averages are used, and intermolecular forces are ignored, which matters for solids and liquids.

notes.heading: Calculating ΔH from bond enthalpies
points: ΔH = Σ(BE bonds broken) − Σ(BE bonds formed), in kJ mol⁻¹.
Draw full structural formulas first so you count the type and number of every bond.
Example C2H4 + HBr → C2H5Br: 2636 − 2701 = −65 kJ mol⁻¹.
Negative result means exothermic: the products have stronger total bonding than the reactants.

notes.heading: Hess's law
points: Enthalpy change is the same whatever route is taken, provided initial and final states are the same.
It applies conservation of energy; enthalpy is a state function.
Summation method: reverse an equation and its ΔH sign changes; multiply the equation and ΔH is multiplied too; add equations and cancel common species.
Cycle method: follow the alternative route; if you go against an arrow, reverse that ΔH's sign.
Show full working so partial marks can be awarded.

notes.heading: Standard enthalpy of combustion and formation
points: ΔHc°: enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in oxygen, standard states.
ΔHf°: enthalpy change when one mole of a substance forms from its elements in their standard states.
Standard conditions here: 298.15 K (25 °C) and 1.00×10⁵ Pa. Write balanced equations with state symbols; fractional coefficients are allowed.
ΔHf° of any element in its standard state is 0; for carbon the most stable allotrope, graphite, is the standard.
Combustion values are in section 14 of the data booklet and formation values in section 13.

notes.heading: Calculating ΔH with formation or combustion data
points: Using formation data: ΔHr° = Σ ΔHf°(products) − Σ ΔHf°(reactants).
Using combustion data: ΔHr° = Σ ΔHc°(reactants) − Σ ΔHc°(products). Note the order is reversed.
Multiply each ΔH by its mole coefficient in the balanced equation before summing.
Example: ΔHf° of pentane from combustion data = 5(−394) + 6(−286) + 3509 = −177 kJ mol⁻¹.
Results from combustion data can differ slightly from booklet values (−177 vs −173), as in the pentane example.

notes.heading: Born–Haber cycles
points: A Born–Haber cycle applies Hess's law to the formation of an ionic compound from its elements.
Steps: atomization, ionization energy, electron affinity, lattice enthalpy, and enthalpy of formation.
Atomization of a solid metal equals its sublimation enthalpy; for a gaseous diatomic it is half the bond enthalpy.
Ionization energy is endothermic (positive); first electron affinity of non-metals is usually negative.
Lattice enthalpy in the IB is endothermic (positive): solid lattice → gaseous ions.
Find an unknown step by the alternative route, reversing the sign for any step taken against its arrow. KBr lattice enthalpy: +687 kJ mol⁻¹.

definitions.definition: Average energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over many compounds, under standard conditions.
definitions.trap: Omitting 'average' or the gaseous state; the definition is often incomplete.

definitions.definition: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final states are the same.
definitions.trap: Forgetting to flip the ΔH sign when reversing an equation, or to multiply it.

definitions.definition: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance in its standard state is burned completely in oxygen under standard conditions.
definitions.trap: Saying 'energy released' rather than enthalpy change, or leaving out one mole.

definitions.definition: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states.
definitions.trap: Saying 'energy required' instead of enthalpy change, or omitting one mole and standard conditions.

definitions.definition: The form a pure substance takes under standard conditions of 298.15 K and 1.00×10⁵ Pa; for carbon, graphite.
definitions.trap: Quoting STP instead of the standard conditions used here.

definitions.definition: The standard enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is removed from one mole of gaseous atoms or positive ions.
definitions.trap: Leaving out gaseous state or saying 'atoms' only, when later ionizations involve ions.

definitions.definition: The standard enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms of an element is formed.
definitions.trap: For a diatomic gas, forgetting it is half the bond enthalpy.

definitions.definition: The standard enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is added to one mole of gaseous atoms.
definitions.trap: Giving it a positive sign; first electron affinity of non-metals is usually negative.

definitions.definition: The standard enthalpy change when gaseous ions are formed from one mole of a solid ionic lattice (endothermic).
definitions.trap: Using the exothermic form (ions to lattice) or giving a negative value; IB uses endothermic.

definitions.definition: An application of Hess's law that combines enthalpy changes for the steps in forming an ionic compound from its elements.
definitions.trap: Not reversing the sign of a step when going against its arrow.
